response.description_long:
Relaymark automates lifecycle messaging for e-commerce brands — the welcome series, abandoned-cart recovery, win-back campaigns, and post-purchase flows that run across email and SMS. The problem it targets is a familiar one in online retail: lifecycle revenue is often claimed by whichever tool touched the customer last, and most email platforms treat retention as a campaign calendar rather than as infrastructure. Relaymark's founding conviction, stated on its site, is that lifecycle revenue is earned by structure rather than volume — the right message at the right hour to the right segment, measured honestly against a holdout.

The product connects to Shopify and BigCommerce, builds a profile of every shopper from orders and browsing events, and runs journeys from a visual builder. Every order, browse, cart event, and message interaction lands on one profile: what a shopper bought, looked at, opened, or ignored. Segments build from any of it — high-AOV repeat buyers, browsers who never purchased, subscribers gone quiet for 90 days — and update in real time as events stream in. Journeys are graphs of triggers, waits, branches, and messages. They can branch on profile data such as cart value, category viewed, prior purchase count, or engagement recency, and on live behavior mid-journey (opened but did not click, clicked but did not buy). Exit rules end a journey the moment its goal is met, so nobody gets a discount email after paying full price, and editing a running flow versions it safely so shoppers mid-journey finish on the version they started.

The flows themselves cover the standard lifecycle jobs. Welcome series greet new subscribers over days and exit early when they buy. Abandoned-cart recovery targets the shopper who left at checkout, with reminders, social proof, and an incentive that escalates only if needed. Win-back campaigns target customers whose purchase cadence has lapsed, and post-purchase flows handle order follow-ups, cross-sells timed to consumption cycles, review requests, and replenishment reminders. Templates encode what works: over 900 brands run on Relaymark, per the site, and the most-copied template is a 4-message abandoned-cart series. The library is organized by vertical and by job — welcome series for considered purchases, cart recovery for impulse categories, replenishment for consumables — and every template ships with its branching logic and timing intact. A/B tests on subject lines, timing, and offers run natively inside flows and are reported as incremental lift with holdout included.

The measurement layer is the sharpest part of the pitch. Relaymark's holdout system keeps a control group per flow and reports true incremental revenue — what the flow earned beyond what would have happened without it — rather than last-click attribution, which the site calls "attribution theater" and the industry disease. Send-time optimization picks each shopper's likely engagement hour and its lift is measured against a control too. Because every flow runs against a holdout, Relaymark publishes aggregate incremental revenue per flow type across its customer base, updated quarterly; the site notes that abandoned-cart recovery leads, welcome series compound, and win-back is the flow most often overrated by last-click math. Brands see their own flows benchmarked against vertical medians in the dashboard, incremental numbers only.

SMS is handled with an explicit eye on its risk profile: consent capture and record-keeping, quiet hours by recipient timezone, frequency caps across flows, and automatic opt-out processing. Email and SMS coordinate inside one journey — a cart reminder texts only if the email went unopened — so shoppers hear one brand rather than two channels competing. Deliverability is treated as product rather than support ticket: dedicated sending infrastructure, warm-up schedules for new domains, bounce and complaint monitoring with automatic throttling, suppression rules that retire unengaged addresses before they hurt the sender score, and a deliverability specialist who reviews every account's first month of sends.

Beyond the two native storefront integrations, Relaymark syncs audiences to Meta and Google ad platforms for suppression and lookalikes, streams every message event to a warehouse via webhooks, and integrates review-request flows with Okendo and Judge.me. It positions itself against the generic ESP, which it says branches on less commerce data, measures by last-click, and shares IP reputation; Relaymark's migration team maps existing automations flow by flow, testing against historical data before cutover, and rebuilds a brand's flows inside two weeks on every plan. Pricing scales with contactable profiles, with email and SMS metered separately, a free tier under 500 profiles, free storage for suppressed and unsubscribed profiles, no annual lock-in, and annual billing discounts.

Relaymark is a 30-person, fully remote company founded in 2020, with customers concentrated in fashion, beauty, and food & beverage. The team came out of e-commerce itself — retention managers, deliverability engineers, and lifecycle marketers who ran these programs by hand at brands and agencies. The site does not disclose funding or revenue figures. Its stated recognition is modest: retention marketing newsletters have covered the holdout methodology as a corrective to last-click claims, and operators cite the quarterly aggregate benchmarks when comparing flow performance across verticals.
